articles.title: I built a Claude Code skill that turns negative competitor reviews into a roadmap
articles.summary: Picking what to build next is the part of running a side project I'm worst at. Open the issue tracker, stare at it, close the issue tracker. Repeat next weekend. A few weeks ago I tried something different: instead of asking myself, I asked the people who already left a competitor. There's a specific kind of useful buried in a 1-star G2 review — someone took the time to write down what they wanted and didn't get. That's a roadmap. The problem is reading hundreds of them. So I built GapHunter, a Claude Code skill that does it for me. You run it like this: /gaphunter DBeaver TablePlus It searches G2, Capterra, TrustRadius, Reddit, GitHub Issues and Hacker News in parallel, clusters near-duplicate complaints (so "no dark mode" and "lacks dark theme" collapse into one finding), then reads your own repo : package.json, Cargo.toml, the src/ tree — and cross-references the gaps against what you've already shipped. articles.title: Extract PDF text in your browser with LiteParse for the web
articles.summary: LlamaIndex have a most excellent open source project called LiteParse, which provides a Node.js CLI tool for extracting text from PDFs. I got a version of LiteParse working entirely in the browser, using most of the same libraries that LiteParse uses to run in Node.js. Spatial text parsing Refreshingly, LiteParse doesn't use AI models to do what it does: it's good old-fashioned PDF parsing, falling back to Tesseract OCR (or other pluggable OCR engines) for PDFs that contain images of text rather than the text itself. The hard problem that LiteParse solves is extracting text in a sensible order despite the infuriating vagaries of PDF layouts. They describe this as "spatial text parsing" - they use some very clever heuristics to detect things like multi-column layouts and group and return the text in a sensible linear flow. I built an EM Operating System using Obsidian (local markdown vault), Claude Code (AI that files and links your notes), and Google Drive (free sync via rclone). It runs on the PARA method — four folders optimised for action, not archiving — and a custom para-capture skill that auto-classifies rough text into the right folder, adds frontmatter, and links related notes.
